## History

The line of descent, oldest first:

- **the elf proto-language**, 20 kyr ago: the reconstructed ancestor (elf).
- **Miplunbyip (elf 6, the south of Ratal)**, 20 kyr ago: continued the proto-language in place (spoken by elf).
- **Kupafi (human 22, the south of Ratal)**, 6.5 kyr ago: formed when the speakers took up another language (spoken by human).
- **Miku (halfling 39, the south of Ratal)**, 0.5 kyr ago: formed when the speakers took up another language.

| | consonants | vowels | tones |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| the elf proto-language, 20 kyr ago | 10: m ɲ p b c k ʔ f h w | 8: i u ɪ e o ɛ ɔ a | 2 |
| now | 13: m n p t̪ k ʔ s f h j w l r | 4: i u e̞ a | none |

**Shift.** 0.5 kyr ago the halfling speakers of deme 704 took up the language of the human (human 22). Trigger: settlements: 3 site(s) of the halfling taken by the human about 2.5 kyr ago (a town or city among them) (settlements.json holders).
From the old language (halfling 39) 24 words were kept, mostly landscape, plants and animals: frog, nest, ox, ripe, caprine (animal), bark, lake, marsh, rooster, snail, spring (of water), tree, desert, forest, ….
The accent the speakers brought (new sound heard as old): c > t̪, iː > i, o̞ > u.
Grammar carried over: polar question initial_particle > intonation; serial verbs no > yes.

**Contact.** Sound changes taken up from neighbours by the wave along the line: halfling 6 (13), halfling 2 (10), elf 9 (6), halfling 21 (5), halfling 2 (5), human 22 (5). Loan events in the present vocabulary (by donor): halfling 39 (161), human 22 (138), halfling 2 (126), elf 6 (103), halfling 21 (63), human 20 (54).

Where symbols share a cell, the voiceless ones come first and the voiced follow the dot. Secondary articulation (ʷ ʲ ˠ ˤ) and length (ː) stay in the cell of the plain sound.

### Vowels

| **Mid** | e̞ |  |

Unrounded vowels come before the dot, rounded after it. Length: no long vowels. Nasality: no nasal vowels.

### Tone, syllables and stress

No phonemic tone.
Syllable shapes (share of syllables in the word-shape model): CV 85%, V 15%. At most 1 consonant(s) before the vowel and 0 after it.
Stress depends on syllable weight (the Latin rule): in longer words it falls on the next-to-last syllable when that is heavy (a long vowel or closed by a consonant), else on the one before; in shorter words on the first. The IPA on this page marks it with ˈ before the stressed syllable.
Core words average 2.45 syllables (4.4 sounds); 35% of words share their form with another word.

## Orthography

The house romanization in two registers: the full spelling (workbench, one letter or digraph per sound, tone marks) and the book spelling (lossy: no tone, plain vowels, and at most 2 diacritic letters kept for the whole language; one spelling per sound in every word). Allophones are spelled as their phonemes.

**Consonants:** m ‹m› · n ‹n› · p ‹p› · t̪ ‹t› · k ‹k› · ʔ ‹'› · s ‹s› · f ‹f› · h ‹h› · j ‹y› · w ‹w› · l ‹l› · r ‹rr›

**Vowels:** i ‹i› · u ‹u› · e̞ ‹e› · a ‹a›

Where two spellings are given the second is the book spelling.

## Grammar

Basic word order is SOV; it has postpositions. In the noun phrase: possessor before the possessed; noun before the adjective; demonstrative before the noun; noun before the numeral; noun before the relative clause. Overall it is head-final.
It has a definite article before the noun, no indefinite article, a few cases, nominative-accusative alignment, singular and plural, a system of noun classes.
Verbs mark past, future and perfective; there are no evidentials. Negation uses a negator before the verb; yes/no questions use a final question particle. Verbs agree with the subject by suffixes; not with the object.
Other features: an inclusive/exclusive 'we' distinction; alienable and inalienable possession told apart; serial verbs; a copula; a bound causative; no passive; question words moved to the front; a decimal counting base.
Measured morphology: 22 live grammatical markers, mean bondedness 1.2 (0 free word … 3 fused), 26 paradigm cells, 7 of them with allomorphy.

### Grammar sketch

Built from the typology and the live markers above (planet/language/sentences.py); where the engine tracks no marker for a construction, the form is the word such markers commonly grow from, and the text says so. Examples are glossed by the Leipzig rules (abbreviations under Sample sentences).

**Number.** Nouns mark number: plural: a suffix (wi, from 'many').

| *mu-aju* |
| --- |
| CL2-dog |

‘dog’

| *mu-aju-wi* |
| --- |
| CL2-dog-PL |

‘dogs’

**Case.** Nouns take 1 case marker: accusative (ACC): a suffix (hi, from the dative marker). Adpositions (free words, not yet case): genitive (GEN): a separate word after the noun phrase (i, from 'that'). Alignment is accusative: the object is marked (ACC), subjects are not.

| *nu* | *i* |
| --- | --- |
| man | GEN |

‘of the man’

| *mu-aju-hi* |
| --- |
| CL2-dog-ACC |

‘the dog (as object)’

**Gender and noun classes.** Nouns are counted with classifiers: class 1 for people (plural of persons), a prefix (mi, from 'people'); class 2 for languages, ways and tools, and for every noun no other class takes, a prefix (mu, from 'tongue'); class 3 for a single person, a separate word before the noun (nuju, from 'person').

| *mu-hijãnu* |
| --- |
| CL2-word |

‘word’

| *nuju* | *nu* |
| --- | --- |
| CL3 | man |

‘man’

**Tense and aspect.** Verbs mark tense and aspect. Past (PST): a clitic after the verb (ua; wua after a back or rounded vowel; from 'yesterday'); perfect (PRF): a separate word after the verb (au, from 'finish'); future (FUT): a clitic after the verb (ku, from 'come'). Unmarked: progressive, habitual (left to context).

| *kuʔu=wua* |
| --- |
| go=PST |

‘(it) went’

| *kuʔu* | *au* |
| --- | --- |
| go | PRF |

‘(it) has gone’

| *kuʔu=ku* |
| --- |
| go=FUT |

‘(it) will go’

**Mood and evidentiality.** No evidential or mood marker is live; statements are unmarked.

**Person agreement.** Verbs agree with the subject: 1SG: a clitic after the verb (ae̞; wae̞ after a back or rounded vowel; from 'I'); 2SG: a clitic after the verb (i; wi after a back or rounded vowel; from 'thou'); 3SG: a clitic after the verb (uwu; wuwu after a back or rounded vowel; from 'he'); 1PL: a clitic after the verb (nuju, from 'person'); 2PL: a clitic after the verb (t̪ĩmi, from 'you'); 3PL: a clitic after the verb (ũnu, from 'they').

| *kuʔu=wae̞* |
| --- |
| go=1SG |

‘I go’

| *kuʔu=wi* |
| --- |
| go=2SG |

‘you go’

| *kuʔu=wuwu* |
| --- |
| go=3SG |

‘he/she goes’

**Negation.** Negation uses the word for 'not' (t̪ahija), preverbal.

| *ae̞* | *i=mu-naufu-hi* | *t̪ahija* | *a=jae̞* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1SG | DEF=CL2-milk-ACC | NEG | drink=1SG |

‘I do not drink the milk.’ (sentence 6 below)

**Questions.** Yes/no questions use a particle at the end of the clause. Question words move to the front: who ilifu, what hu, where hua, when t̪ije̞, how huru.

| *i* | *i=mu-hipu-hi* | *lĩma=ji* | *hi* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2SG | DEF=CL2-thunder-ACC | hear=2SG | Q |

‘Do you hear the thunder?’ (sentence 4 below)

| *hu-hi* | *i=nukuwu* | *ĩmĩme̞ku=wuwu* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| what-ACC | DEF=child | bring=3SG |

‘What does the child bring?’ (sentence 5 below)

**Commands.** There is no imperative marker: a command is the bare verb stem, with no subject and no subject or tense marker.

| *i=mu-hi-hi* | *siʔũma* |
| --- | --- |
| DEF=CL2-fish-ACC | eat |

‘Eat the fish!’ (sentence 12 below)

**Possession.** The possessor stands before the possessed noun, marked by the genitive marker, a separate word after the noun phrase (i). Kin and body parts (inalienable) take no genitive marker. 'Having' is said with 'with' ('my mother is with a boat').

| *i=nu* | *i* | *mu-aju* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| DEF=man | GEN | CL2-dog |

‘the man's dog’

| *ae̞* | *lifu* | *mu-lulũnau* | *lifĩma-je̞* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1SG | mother | CL2-boat | with-COP |

‘My mother has a boat.’ (sentence 7 below)

**Relative clauses.** Relative clause after the noun, introduced by the word for 'that' (as English that and German der grew from a pointing word).

| *i=lifu* | *ĩmi* | *hiju=wuwu* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| DEF=woman | REL | dance=3SG |

‘the woman who dances’

**Copula.** The copula is a suffix (e̞; je̞ after a front or central vowel; we̞ after a back or rounded vowel; from 'that').

| *ĩmi* | *nu* | *miwu-we̞* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| that | man | merchant-COP |

‘That man is a merchant.’ (sentence 9 below)

| *i=mu-sa* | *mut̪uhi-je̞* |
| --- | --- |
| DEF=CL2-water | cold-COP |

‘the water is cold’

**Pronouns.** 'We' has two forms: inclusive a (you and I, the hearer among us) and exclusive hu (we, but not you).

| *a* |
| --- |
| 1PL.INCL |

‘we (you included)’

| *hu* |
| --- |
| 1PL.EXCL |

‘we (not you)’

| *a* | *i=mu-hi-hi* | *siʔũma=nuju* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1PL.INCL | DEF=CL2-fish-ACC | eat=1PL |

‘We (you and I) eat the fish.’ (sentence 14 below)

**Serial verbs.** Verbs can be strung together in one clause with one subject (serial verbs): 'take X come' is 'bring'. 'Go' after a motion verb gives its direction ('run go' = run away).

| *i=nu* | *i=mu-hi-hi* | *ifufu=wuwu* | *ĩmĩme̞* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| DEF=man | DEF=CL2-fish-ACC | take=3SG | come |

‘The man brings the fish (takes it and comes).’ (sentence 13 below)

| *it̪ãmãmu* | *kuʔu* |
| --- | --- |
| run | go |

‘run away’

**Giving (two objects).** No dative: a serial construction, 'take the thing, give (it to) the person'.

| *i=lifu* | *i=mu-hi-hi* | *ifufu=wuwu* | *i=nukuwu* | *u* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| DEF=woman | DEF=CL2-fish-ACC | take=3SG | DEF=child | give |

‘The woman gives the child a fish.’ (sentence 11 below)

**Numerals.** Counting is decimal: numbers above ten are built from ten and the units. Twenty is muʔuku and a hundred is ha.

| *t̪ãmiʔia* |
| --- |
| 11 |

‘11 = 10 + 1 ('ten' and 'one')’

| *mĩmuʔu* |
| --- |
| 15 |

‘15 = 10 + 5 ('ten' and 'five')’

| *muʔũmu* |
| --- |
| 30 |

‘30 = 10 × 3 ('ten' and 'three')’

**Concord.** The noun's class marker is copied onto demonstratives and adjectives (agreement in class, as in Bantu and in Indo-European gender).

| *mu-wĩmi* | *mu-aju* | *mu-hĩmĩmi* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CL2-that | CL2-dog | CL2-big |

‘that big dog’

**Linking clauses.** Complement clauses stand bare, with no complementizer.

| *i=nu* | *i=mu-aju* | *sijau=wuwu* | *ijmãmĩma=juwu* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| DEF=man | DEF=CL2-dog | sleep=3SG | say=3SG |

‘The man says that the dog sleeps.’ (sentence 15 below)

**Topic and focus.** Topic and focus are marked: topic (TOP): a clitic after the noun phrase (i; ji after a front or central vowel; from 'that').

| *i=mu-hi=ji* | *i=nu* | *siʔũma=juwu* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| DEF=CL2-fish=TOP | DEF=man | eat=3SG |

‘The fish, the man eats it.’ (sentence 16 below)

**Word shapes.** Some markers sound the same: DEF and TOP are both i (context tells them apart).

**Demonstratives.** Demonstratives count two distances: 'this' lijaĩnijae̞ (near) and 'that' ĩmi (far).

| *mu-lijaĩnijae̞* | *mu-aju* |
| --- | --- |
| CL2-this | CL2-dog |

‘this dog’

| *mu-wĩmi* | *mu-aju* |
| --- | --- |
| CL2-that | CL2-dog |

‘that dog’

**Comparison.** A conjoined comparison: 'A is big, B is small' (no comparative construction, as in many languages of New Guinea and Australia).

| *i=nu* | *hĩmĩmi-je̞* | *i=mu-aju* | *ae̞ri-je̞* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| DEF=man | big-COP | DEF=CL2-dog | small-COP |

‘The man is bigger than the dog.’ (sentence 17 below)

### Colour terms

Berlin & Kay stage V: 6 basic colour words (white; black; red; yellow/brown; green; blue).

### Families a speaker feels

The roots a speaker still feels: a derivation or compound younger than 3 kyr whose parts are still in use (per-word `roots`). 16 families of 3+ words; 20% of the 769 words share a root with another word.

The largest: **night** *ma˦wa˦m* (N, coined 20 kyr ago in the elf proto-language); 3 words have it as their main root, 4 contain it.

| meaning | IPA | spelling | roots (main first) | how it was built |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| dark | mahi | mahi | night | \*ma˦wa˦m 'night' (the elf proto-language, 20 kyr) → NIGHT + 'like' = 'dark' (2.5) |
| darkness | mahĩnu | mahinu | night | \*ma˦wa˦m 'night' (the elf proto-language, 20 kyr) → NIGHT + 'like' = 'dark' (2.5) → DARK + 'thing' = 'darkness' (1.5) |
| night | ma | ma | night | \*ma˦wa˦m 'night' (the elf proto-language, 20 kyr) |
| dew | mara | marra | water, night | coined ja 'raining or rain' (6) → 'raining or rain' > 'water' (3) → WATER + NIGHT = 'dew' (1) |

### Families a historian reconstructs

The roots a historian reconstructs: every word's family as it was when the word was made, carried forward however opaque it has become since (per-word `etym_roots`, the *bher- 'carry' > burden view). 69 families of 3+ words; 58% of the 769 words share a root with another word.

The largest: **carry** *ku˨he˨kɛ˦pɔ˦m* (V, coined 20 kyr ago in the elf proto-language); 11 words have it as their main root, 15 contain it.

## Names of people and places

**Naming tradition.** Given names are two themes from a closed pool, compounded (as Germanic *Wil-helm*, Slavic *Vladi-mir*); the byname is an epithet after the name. The tradition goes back to the elf proto-language. Themes: first bear, good, land, love, rich, strong, water, wolf; second gift, head, help, king, spear, strong.

| name | IPA | meaning | | etymology |
\|---\|---\|---\|---\|---\|
| **Hefimeifeta** | /he̞fĩme̞ife̞t̪a/ | 'good-help' | old, opaque | Hefimeifeta 'good-help': hefimeku 'good'; the root is now 'true' + ifeta 'help'; the root is now 'servant'; an old name, coined in d550 4.0 kyr ago as Si̱ii̱e |
| **Hefimehimiye** | /he̞fĩme̞hĩmije̞/ | 'good-gift' | old, opaque | Hefimehimiye 'good-gift': hefimeku 'good'; the root is now 'true' + himiye 'gift'; an old name, coined in d550 4.0 kyr ago as Si̱isimi |
| **Tia** | /t̪ia/ | 'strong-head' | old, opaque | Tia 'strong-head': ti 'strong'; the word is gone from the language + apwihiya 'head'; the root is now 'knee'; an old name, coined in d550 4.0 kyr ago as Kyisibi, worn down in use |
| **Hulumuta** | /hulũmut̪a/ | 'strong-king' | new | Hulumuta 'strong-king': hu 'strong' + lumuta 'king'; coined from today's words |
| **Huihinu** | /huihĩnu/ | 'strong-spear' | new | Huihinu 'strong-spear': hu 'strong' + ihinu 'spear'; coined from today's words |
| **Unu'uiyu** | /ũnuʔuiju/ | 'rich-head' | new | Unu'uiyu 'rich-head': unu'u 'rich' + iyu 'head'; coined from today's words |
| **Hefimeifeta Utuni** | /he̞fĩme̞ife̞t̪a ʔut̪ũni/ | 'good-help, the black' | epithet | utuni 'black', a byname |
| **Hefimehimiye Teimihi** | /he̞fĩme̞hĩmije̞ t̪e̞ĩmihi/ | 'good-gift, the red' | epithet | teimihi 'red', a byname |

**Settlements.** **Yuyuwe** /jujuwe̞/ (town, 9,781): 'the big town'; from town (worn to a suffix), founded 8.7 kyr ago; **Nepayi** /ne̞paji/ (town, 9,400): 'the long fence'; named by the halfling (d704) who founded it 8.7 kyr ago, kept as heard; **Yipisu** /jipisu/ (town, 3,400): 'Ich'uhe's fence'; named by the human (d561) who founded it 8.7 kyr ago, kept as heard.

Built from this language's own words, word order, markers and agreement (planet/language/sentences.py). Each has the form line (‘-’ an affix boundary, ‘=’ a clitic boundary), a morpheme-by-morpheme gloss, the free translation, then the whole sentence in IPA (after the simple joining rules: a glide between two vowels, a nasal taking the place of a following stop) and in the book spelling. Nothing here is attested speech; it is what the grammar data implies.

## Texts

Each sentence in four lines: the book spelling, the IPA with its morph breaks, the gloss, and the English.

### A fable: The Bird and the Fish

One fixed short fable, told in every language as August Schleicher told his in Proto-Indo-European (1868), so that the same text shows what sound change and grammar change did. English: A bird sat in a tree. The bird saw a fish in the water. The bird said: “Come! I will give you a good seed.” The fish said: “I do not eat seeds. You will eat me.” The fish did not come. The bird ate the seed.
